extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and IP practitioners (UK-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the UKIPO assesses patentability of computer-implemented inventions, including AI and quantum-computing inventions, under Section 1 of the Manual of Patent Practice. Useful for drafting and prosecuting UK patent applications in these technical areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of inventions (Section 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1 relates to the patentability of inventions; defining which inventions can and cannot be successfully patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This manual section lays out the UKIPO’s approach to examination of patentability; the updates clarify how computer-related inventions are assessed. The guidance should be used to determine whether an invention falls within exclusions or satisfies the requirements for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer is defined as "a machine which processes information".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is broad and means that many devices/systems that process information may be treated as computers for patentability analysis, widening the scope of computer-program exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a computer program
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer program is "a set of instructions for a computer to do something" and any "set of instructions for processing information".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this is a broad definition, the corresponding exclusions to patentability (e.g., computer programs as such) can potentially encompass a wide range of inventions. Applicants should be aware that program-like elements may trigger exclusion analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical contribution requirement for computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical contribution (a technical effect) is the essential characteristic required for a computer-implemented invention to be considered patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Manual provides clearer guidance and examples of what constitutes a technical contribution. Examiners will seek a technical effect or technical contribution beyond mere excluded subject-matter (e.g., a mere computer program or mathematical method). Applications should identify and emphasize technical effects arising from the implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: AT&T signposts (five indicators) for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manual cites cases with respect to the five indicators (the so‑called AT&T signposts, from [2009] EWHC 343 (Pat)) for determining whether a computer-implemented invention is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of the five signposts is discussed with case relevance in more detail than previously. Practitioners should review the signposts and associated case law to map an invention to indicators of technical contribution; the Manual explains the relevance of those cases to current practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of AI inventions as computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because practical implementations of AI inventions typically rely on computers, the Manual considers AI inventions should be interpreted as computer-implemented inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accordingly, AI inventions are to be judged against the criteria for computer-implemented inventions (i.e., require a technical contribution). The Manual adopts the position that AI implementations fall within the same exclusion/assessment framework as other computer programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned weights treated as computer program (AI-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manual indicates the learned weights are the computer program, as it is these which instruct a machine executing the ANN on how to convert an input into a particular output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses arguments (e.g., in the Emotional Perception case) that ANNs are not programs because there are no explicit instructions; examiners may treat trained model parameters/weights as the 'instructions' for patentability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI inventions may be regarded as mathematical in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance indicates that AI inventions are considered to be mathematical in nature, offering the UKIPO another avenue for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiners view an AI invention as essentially a mathematical method (an excluded category), it may be rejected on that basis even if also treated as computer-implemented. Applicants should identify technical application/technical effects to avoid a pure-mathematical characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum computing inventions assessed like other computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantum computing inventions are to be treated in the same manner as any other computer-implemented invention because a quantum computer is still "a machine which processes information".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain a patent in the quantum area, it is necessary to identify a technical effect resulting from the execution of a program by a quantum computer. The Manual references detection and correction of errors as an example of a relevant technical effect. Given the novelty of the field there are few positive examples; three decisions are cited where no technical contribution was found.
